title: Are expert reports admissible at trial?
summary: Are expert reports admissible at trial? Learn the federal hearsay baseline, permitted uses, and how Rules 703, 705, and 801–803 apply in patent cases.
body_markdown:
In U.S. federal court, a written expert report offered to prove its assertions usually presents a hearsay problem. It does not become evidence simply because its author testifies, the opinion satisfies Rule 702, or the report was disclosed under Rule 26. Its treatment still depends on the purpose of offer, an applicable nonhearsay rule or exception, foundation, stipulations, orders, and the court’s rulings.


Patent teams should separate the expert's testimony, the material supporting the opinion, and the written report itself. State evidence law, local rules, case orders, and the trial judge's rulings may produce a different answer.


## Key takeaways


- **The report and the testimony are different evidence.** A court may admit the expert's live opinion without receiving the report as a substantive exhibit.
- **Purpose comes first.** Truth, basis of opinion, refreshing recollection, impeachment, completeness, and illustration invoke different rules.
- **Rule 703 is not an exhibit shortcut.** Permissible reliance on inadmissible facts or data does not make those materials, or the report, evidence for their truth.
- **Rule 26 is a disclosure rule.** A required expert report does not automatically become an admitted trial exhibit.
- **Hearsay is only one gate.** Authentication, relevance, Rule 403, stipulations, pretrial orders, and any embedded hearsay still matter.


## Start with what is being offered and why


The phrase “expert report” can hide several distinct trial requests. Identify the item and the purpose before choosing the rule.


What the proponent wants to use Primary question Starting rule Evidentiary status


The expert's live opinion May this witness give this opinion? Rules 702, 703, and 705 Testimony if admitted; the report does not follow automatically


The written report for its assertions Is an out-of-court written statement being offered for its truth? Rules 801 and 802 Usually hearsay unless a valid route applies


Facts or data supporting the opinion May the expert rely on them, disclose them, or both? Rule 703 Reliance and jury disclosure are separate from substantive admission


A chart, slide, or technical diagram Is it an illustrative aid or proof of voluminous admissible material? Rules 107 and 1006 An aid is not evidence; a qualifying Rule 1006 summary can be


A prior statement in the report Is it used to refresh, impeach, complete a partial presentation, or prove truth? Rules 612, 613, 106, and 801–803 The purpose and predicates control


The court decides preliminary admissibility questions under Rule 104(a). The item also must be relevant, authenticated when required, and survive Rule 403. The[current Federal Rules of Evidence](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-evidence.pdf) supply those separate gates.


## Why a written expert report usually raises hearsay


Rule 801 defines a statement to include a written assertion. It defines hearsay as a statement the declarant did not make while testifying at the current trial or hearing, offered to prove what the statement asserts. Rule 802 excludes hearsay unless a federal statute, the Evidence Rules, or another Supreme Court rule provides otherwise.


A signed report therefore remains an out-of-court statement even when its author later takes the stand. The expert's availability for cross-examination does not, standing alone, remove the report from the[Rules 801 and 802](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-evidence.pdf) .


The purpose can change the analysis. A sentence offered only to show an inconsistency may support impeachment without proving that sentence true. A related passage may be needed to correct a misleading partial presentation. A report may also contain statements from product documents, testing personnel, license records, or other experts. Rule 805 requires an admissible route for each layer when those embedded statements are offered for their truth.


## An admissible expert opinion is different from an admitted report


Three expert-testimony rules answer three different questions:


- **Rule 702 addresses the testimony.** The proponent must establish, more likely than not, that the expert is qualified, the specialized knowledge will help the factfinder, the testimony rests on sufficient facts or data, the principles and methods are reliable, and the opinion reflects a reliable application to the case.
- **Rule 703 addresses the opinion's basis and possible jury disclosure.** Experts may rely on facts or data that need not themselves be admissible if experts in the field reasonably rely on that kind of material. The proponent may disclose otherwise inadmissible facts or data to the jury only when their value in helping the jury evaluate the opinion substantially outweighs their prejudicial effect.
- **Rule 705 addresses order of proof.** Unless the court orders otherwise, an expert may state the opinion and reasons before testifying to the underlying facts or data. Cross-examination may require their disclosure.


None of those provisions is a hearsay exception for the written report. The[official Rules 702, 703, and 705](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-evidence.pdf) keep testimony, reliance, disclosure, and the sequence of proof distinct.


Official U.S. Courts excerpt of Evidence Rules 703 and 705, 1200 × 672.


*Rules 703 and 705, cropped from the[official U.S. Courts rules](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-evidence.pdf) (December 1, 2025 edition). Rule 704, which appears between them in the source PDF, is omitted.*


Patent damages illustrate the separate Rule 702 gate. In *EcoFactor, Inc. v. Google LLC* , No. 23-1101 (Fed. Cir. May 21, 2025), the en banc Federal Circuit held that the district court abused its discretion by admitting a damages opinion that lacked sufficient factual support on the record before it. The court reversed the denial of a new damages trial and remanded. The[en banc EcoFactor opinion](https://www.cafc.uscourts.gov/opinions-orders/23-1101.OPINION.5-21-2025_2518737.pdf) concerns the reliability of expert testimony. It does not make a Rule 26 report an admissible exhibit.


## Does Rule 26 make the report trial evidence?


No. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26 governs disclosure, not substantive admissibility.


Rule 26(a)(2)(B) requires a written report prepared and signed by a retained or specially employed expert, and by a party employee whose duties regularly involve giving expert testimony, unless the court orders or the parties stipulate otherwise. Rule 26(a)(2)(C) instead requires a subject-matter and facts-and-opinions summary for a witness who is not required to provide a report.


The rule separately requires pretrial identification of documents and other exhibits a party may present, and it provides a process for admissibility objections. Discovery can also reach relevant, proportional information that need not be admissible. The[Rule 26 expert-disclosure text](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-civil-procedure.pdf) therefore does not convert discovery disclosure into an evidentiary ruling.


The scheduling order, final pretrial order, local rules, standing orders, stipulations, and rulings on motions in limine control the matter-specific process. Rule 26(a)(3)(B) separately governs objections to listed trial exhibits. Unless the court sets a different time, an admissibility objection not made within 14 days after the pretrial disclosure is waived—except an objection under Evidence Rule 402 or 403—unless the court excuses the omission for good cause. Listing the report does not itself make it admissible or create a hearsay exception.


## Routes and limited uses that can change the analysis


No single exception covers expert reports as a category. Each route has its own purpose, predicates, and limits.


### Opposing-party statements under Rule 801(d)(2)


A statement offered against an opposing party is nonhearsay when the party made it, adopted it, authorized the speaker to make it, or when the listed agency or employee conditions are met. Retaining an expert does not automatically establish adoption, authority, or agency.


The cases turn on the record. In *Collins v. Wayne Corp.* , 621 F.2d 777, 781–82 (5th Cir. 1980), the Fifth Circuit treated an accident investigator's report and deposition as the company's statements after finding that the company employed him to investigate and analyze that accident. The[Collins agency finding](https://openjurist.org/621/f2d/777) was fact specific. In *Kirk v. Raymark Industries, Inc.* , 61 F.3d 147, 163–64 (3d Cir. 1995), the Third Circuit rejected automatic attribution where the expert was not subject to the retaining party's control or authorized to speak for it. The[Kirk analysis](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/61/147/492748/) requires a controlling-jurisdiction and record-specific inquiry.


### Recorded recollection under Rule 803(5)


Recorded recollection requires proof that the witness once knew the matter, now cannot recall it well enough to testify fully and accurately, made or adopted the record while the matter was fresh, and accurately recorded that knowledge. If admitted, the record may be read into evidence. It may be received as an exhibit only when the adverse party offers it.


An expert's memory lapse does not make the entire report a recorded recollection. Each predicate still needs support.


### Business records under Rule 803(6)


A business-record theory requires a record made at or near the time by—or from information transmitted by—someone with knowledge, kept in a regularly conducted activity, made as a regular practice, supported by a qualified witness or compliant certification, and not shown by the opponent to lack trustworthiness.


Litigation preparation creates a serious fit problem, but no categorical rule bars every expert-related record. In *Paddack v. Dave Christensen, Inc.* , 745 F.2d 1254, 1257–60 (9th Cir. 1984), the Ninth Circuit rejected business-record treatment for special compliance audits commissioned after suspected irregularities and prepared in anticipation of litigation. The court also rejected Rule 1006 admission on that record because the proponent had not established admissible underlying material and access.[Paddack 's special-audit ruling](https://openjurist.org/745/f2d/1254/paddack-v-dave-christensen-inc-h) does not hold that every report associated with an expert fails Rule 803(6).


### Learned treatises under Rule 803(18)


Rule 803(18) covers a qualifying statement in a treatise, periodical, or pamphlet when it is relied on during direct examination or called to an expert's attention on cross-examination, and the publication is established as a reliable authority through the rule's permitted methods. The statement may be read into evidence. The publication is not received as an exhibit.


A retained expert's advocacy report does not become a learned treatise because an expert wrote it.


### Refreshing recollection under Rule 612


When a witness uses a writing to refresh memory while testifying, Rule 612 entitles the adverse party to production, inspection, cross-examination, and introduction of portions related to the testimony. The same options apply to a writing used before testimony if the court decides that justice requires them. The proponent's use of the report to refresh memory does not automatically place it in evidence for its truth.


Rule 612 is also distinct from Rule 803(5). Refreshed recollection produces testimony from present memory. Recorded recollection permits the qualifying record to be read when memory remains insufficient.


### Impeachment under Rule 613


A prior report can support impeachment when it materially conflicts with the expert's testimony. Rule 613 governs examination about the prior statement and, unless the court orders otherwise, requires an opportunity for the witness to explain or deny it and for the adverse party to examine the witness before extrinsic evidence is admitted.


Impeachment attacks credibility. Substantive use for truth needs another route. As of September 26, 2026, current Rule 801(d)(1)(A) treats an inconsistent prior statement as nonhearsay only when the declarant testifies and is subject to cross-examination, and the earlier statement was made under penalty of perjury at a trial, hearing, other proceeding, or deposition. A signed Rule 26 report does not necessarily meet those conditions.


U.S. Courts lists a Rule 801(d)(1)(A) amendment as projected to take effect December 1, 2026, but warns that projected amendments can be delayed or withdrawn. If the amendment takes effect as projected, it would remove the sworn-prior-proceeding condition for an inconsistent statement by a declarant who testifies and is subject to cross-examination. The proposed text remains subject to Rule 403, leaves Rule 613's extrinsic-evidence requirements in place, and would govern later proceedings plus pending proceedings when just and practicable. The[pending-amendments page](https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/pending-rules-and-forms-amendments) explains the current status, and the[2026 congressional rules package](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/2026_congressional_package_final.pdf) contains the proposed text and effective-date provision.


### Completeness under Rule 106


If a party introduces part of a statement, Rule 106 permits the adverse party to require another part or a related statement at the same time when fairness requires it, even over a hearsay objection. The proponent should identify the misleading partial presentation and the material needed to correct it. Mentioning one report sentence does not create a right to admit the entire report.


### Stipulations, orders, and bench trials


A stipulation or court order can change which objections remain contested and how expert evidence is presented. The scope matters. Determine whether the agreement covers identity, authenticity, hearsay, substantive truth, a limited purpose, use with the jury, or only inclusion on an exhibit list.


A bench trial does not automatically make the report admissible. A judge may manage evidence differently from a jury trial, and the parties may agree to use reports as direct testimony, but the governing order and preserved objections still control.


## Demonstratives and Rule 1006 summaries are different


Rule 107 allows an illustrative aid when its help to the factfinder is not substantially outweighed by the listed risks. The aid is not evidence and ordinarily does not go to the jury during deliberations, unless all parties consent or the court finds good cause.


Rule 1006 addresses a different item. A court may admit a summary, chart, or calculation to prove the content of voluminous admissible writings, recordings, or photographs that cannot conveniently be examined in court. The underlying originals or duplicates must be available to the other parties at a reasonable time and place. The[Rules 107 and 1006 text](https://www.uscourts.gov/sites/default/files/document/federal-rules-of-evidence.pdf) expressly separates evidentiary summaries from illustrative aids.


In a patent case, a technical diagram used to explain source-code testimony may be an illustrative aid. A calculation summarizing voluminous admissible license records may qualify under Rule 1006. A claim-chart excerpt could be evidence, an aid, a summary, or a basis for an opinion depending on what it is offered to prove and the foundation established. Calling any of them a “summary” does not select the evidentiary route. The same distinction applies to[source-linked claim charts](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/submission-ready-claim-charts-with-ai) prepared for litigation.


## A patent-litigation issue list for trial preparation


Technical experts may address source code, product documents, testing, licensing data, or damages inputs. Each source keeps its own admissibility path. The report does not absorb those paths, and the expert's reliance does not cure a source's independent defect.


Review these questions with trial counsel:


1. What exact item is being offered, by whom, and for what purpose?
2. Is the proponent seeking live testimony, a substantive exhibit, a limited-purpose use, or an illustrative aid?
3. What nonhearsay route or exception applies to each assertion and each embedded statement offered for truth?
4. Can the team establish relevance, authenticity, and a response to any Rule 403 issue?
5. If Rule 703 material is involved, is reliance reasonable in the field, and is any proposed jury disclosure separately supportable?
6. Are the report author, underlying documents, technical evidence, accused versions or configurations, testing conditions, and pinpoint citations preserved for foundation and cross-examination?
7. What do the scheduling order, exhibit list, motions in limine, final pretrial order, local rules, stipulations, and prior rulings actually provide?


For technical proof, a generic product name is rarely enough. Tie the record to the identified product version, configuration, date, author or custodian, collection method, and source. ## Frequently asked questions


### Are expert reports admissible at trial?


It depends on the purpose for which the report is offered. In U.S. federal court, a written expert report offered to prove its assertions usually raises hearsay under Rules 801 and 802. Live expert testimony is a separate form of evidence. A nonhearsay use, applicable exception, adequate foundation, stipulation, or court order may change the report's treatment.


### Does Rule 703 make an expert report admissible?


No. Rule 703 may permit an expert to base an admissible opinion on facts or data that are not independently admissible if experts in the field reasonably rely on that kind of material. Disclosure of otherwise inadmissible material to the jury faces a separate heightened balance, and admitting the written report as an exhibit still requires its own evidentiary route.


### Does a Rule 26 expert report automatically become a trial exhibit?


No. Rule 26 governs expert disclosures. Rule 26(a)(2)(B) requires reports from retained or specially employed experts and certain employee experts, while Rule 26(a)(2)(C) requires a summary disclosure for witnesses who do not have to provide a report. Trial-exhibit identification and admissibility objections are separate.


### Can an expert use a report to refresh recollection?


Potentially. Rule 612 permits a writing to refresh a witness's memory and gives the adverse party rights to production, inspection, cross-examination, and introduction of related portions. The expert's review of the report does not automatically make the report the proponent's substantive evidence.


### Can an expert report be used to impeach the expert?


Potentially. A materially inconsistent report can be used subject to Rule 613's procedures. As of September 26, 2026, truth use under current Rule 801(d)(1)(A) requires a sworn prior statement at a qualifying proceeding. A pending amendment is projected for December 1, 2026, but may be delayed or withdrawn. If it takes effect, the amendment would remove that condition for an inconsistent statement by a testifying declarant who is subject to cross-examination, subject to Rule 403.


### Is an opposing party's expert report a party admission?


Not automatically. Rule 801(d)(2) requires proof of adoption, authorization, or a qualifying agency or employee relationship and scope. Courts have treated retained experts differently on different facts, so the record and controlling jurisdiction matter.


### Is an expert report a learned treatise?


No, merely labeling work as expert analysis does not make it a learned treatise. Rule 803(18) applies to qualifying statements in a treatise, periodical, or pamphlet after the required examination and reliable-authority foundation. The statement may be read into evidence, while the publication itself is not received as an exhibit.


### Can the jury see an expert demonstrative or summary?


The court controls that use. A Rule 107 illustrative aid may help the jury understand evidence, but it is not evidence and ordinarily does not go to deliberations. A Rule 1006 summary may be admitted to prove the content of voluminous admissible materials if the rule's access and foundation requirements are satisfied.
